summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), which MPLS routers use to tell each other which labels to use. It lets operators monitor LDP sessions, peers and label mappings, and configure some of them, using standard management tools.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers agree on little sticker codes for packages by chatting with neighbors. This document defines a standard report card so a manager can see who is chatting and what codes they agreed on.

subtitle: Four SNMP MIB modules that let operators watch and configure LDP sessions, peers and labels on MPLS routers.

tldr.problem: Routers that use the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) to set up MPLS paths had no standard way for network management systems to see or configure LDP sessions, peers and label state.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four MIB modules: a common one for all LDP implementations, plus one each for Ethernet-style generic labels, ATM and Frame Relay. Each has tables for entities, peers, sessions, statistics and notifications.
tldr.outcome: Operators can use ordinary SNMP tools to configure potential LDP sessions and monitor running ones. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

facts.label: Notifications defined
facts.value: 4 LDP-specific notifications named in the text

today: RFC 3815 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Management Framework
sections.content:
RFC 3815 defines four MIB modules that together support configuring and monitoring the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). LDP, defined in RFC 3036, is one of the MPLS protocols described in RFC 3031 and RFC 3032. Using all four modules lets an operator configure LDP sessions over three Layer 2 media: Ethernet, ATM and Frame Relay.

A MIB (Management Information Base) is a virtual information store whose objects are normally accessed with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The modules are written in SMIv2 and follow the Internet-Standard Management Framework summarized in RFC 3410. The RFC does not teach MPLS itself and points readers to RFC 3031, RFC 3037 and RFC 3215 for background.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a classroom scoreboard that every teacher agrees to use. This document is the agreed layout of the scoreboard for routers that hand out label codes.

sections.title: How the Four Modules Fit Together
sections.content:
The MPLS-LDP-STD-MIB holds objects common to all LDP implementations. Three Layer 2 modules add what is specific to each medium: MPLS-LDP-GENERIC-STD-MIB (per-platform label space), MPLS-LDP-ATM-STD-MIB and MPLS-LDP-FRAME-RELAY-STD-MIB.

An agent on a Label Switching Router (LSR) or Label Edge Router (LER) MUST implement the common module and at least one Layer 2 module. For example, LDP over Ethernet needs the common and generic modules, and an implementation that uses all three media must support all four.

Each module has two compliance statements. Full compliance allows both configuration and monitoring through SNMP. Read-only compliance allows monitoring only.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one main rulebook and three add-on pages, one for each kind of road. A router needs the main rulebook and the add-on for the roads it really uses.

sections.title: The Core Tables of the Common Module
sections.content:
The mplsLdpEntityTable is where an LSR is configured to start or accept LDP sessions. Each row is one LDP Entity. Before creating one, a management station should read mplsLdpEntityIndexNext; a value of zero means the router cannot create another entity right now.

Most other tables are filled in by the agent as the protocol runs. The mplsLdpPeerTable (read-only) describes peers learned through discovery or initialization. The mplsLdpSessionTable (read-only) has one row per session between an entity and a peer, and rows appear during session initialization. The Hello Adjacency table lists adjacencies, and a session with zero adjacencies has lost contact with its peer and should be removed.

Statistics tables help with troubleshooting. If the counter mplsLdpEntityStatsSessionRejectedLRErrors keeps rising, the label range may need adjusting. The mplsLdpSessionPeerAddrTable stores addresses learned through Address Message advertisement.

Only the FEC tables, mplsFecTable and mplsLdpLspFecTable, can be configured by the operator to give Forwarding Equivalence Class information for an LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: One list says which friends this router is willing to talk to. Other lists, filled in by the router itself, show who it is actually talking to and how well the talks are going.

sections.title: Changing a Running Session
sections.content:
If an object used in session initialization is changed after initialization has started, the whole session must be halted and anything learned from it discarded. The RFC gives a worked example for changing a label range on an established session.

The operator sets mplsLdpEntityAdminStatus to disable(2), which tears the session down. The agent then removes the related peer and session rows and, if the optional LSR MIB mapping tables are implemented, the related LSP information as well. The operator edits the label range and sets the status back to enable(1), and session initialization runs again to tell the peer about the new range.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to change the rules of a game already in progress, you stop the game, change the rules, and start over from the beginning.

sections.title: LSPs, Layer 2 Modules and Notifications
sections.content:
Label information lives in the LSR MIB (RFC 3813), in its cross-connect, in-segment and out-segment tables. This MIB adds mplsInSegmentLdpLspTable and mplsOutSegmentLdpLspTable to link LDP sessions to the LSPs they created. These two tables are optional and only needed if the LSR MIB tables are implemented.

The ATM and Frame Relay modules each have two configuration tables and one read-only session table. The configuration tables hold information that would appear in the Optional Parameter and Label Range parts of an LDP Initialization Message. The generic module has a label range table, mplsLdpEntityGenericLRTable, for reserving generic labels.

Four notifications are defined: mplsLdpInitSessionThresholdExceeded (a session keeps failing to start; a threshold of 0 means infinity and the notification is never sent), mplsLdpPathVectorLimitMismatch (entity and peer disagree on the Path Vector Limit; the session uses the entity's value), mplsLdpSessionUp and mplsLdpSessionDown. The working group kept up and down as separate notifications because some management applications match them more easily that way. The RFC expects notifications to be few in a stable network and says a throttling object may be added later if that proves wrong.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB can ring a bell when a friendship starts, ends, or can never get started. It keeps the bells separate so the manager can tell them apart easily.

sections.title: Differences from the LDP Specification
sections.content:
The RFC lists three places where it departs from RFC 3036. First, the entity table has DEFVAL defaults that the LDP specification does not state; they were adopted because existing MIB implementations widely used them, and they can be changed at row creation or by a later SET. Second, the generic label range table does not exist in the LDP specification and was added at the working group's request. Third, a textual convention in RFC 3811 restricts ATM VCI values to be greater than 31, as in RFC 3035.

VPNs and multicast are left out because the LDP specification does not cover them. They would have to be specified there first.
sections.plainLanguage: The scoreboard copies the official rulebook almost exactly. It lists the three small places where it adds its own touches.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Writable objects, such as those in the entity table and the LSP-to-FEC table, can disrupt traffic if an unauthorized party changes them, especially once a session is established. Readable objects can reveal the LDP LSP topology of the network, so even GET and notification access may need control or encryption.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED, and requires SNMPv3 VACM and USM for any v3 agent implementing the common module. It is the operator's job to give access only to legitimate users.
sections.plainLanguage: The scoreboard shows how the roads connect and lets people change settings. So only trusted people should get the key to it.
